purpose: The Server's execution context, replayed. Each case carries the op (without the schema wrapper) and the answer the kernel must give: the parsed answer, or {"error": "<the exact Err string>"} when the request itself is malformed. ds-web replays the same file through the vendored WASM, so no rule about who may see, admit, keep, queue or recover a project's work can be true on one host and not another.
source: ds-web/docs/project-and-instance-isolation-contract.md (One verified context per operation; Server jobs and multiple clients; Concurrency and capacity; acceptance items 2, 5, 6, 7, 8), 2026-09-12.
note: Re-record expected with DS_EXECUTION_CONTEXT_CASES_WRITE=1 cargo test --test execution_context_cases after a deliberate rule change, and say why in the commit.

cases.why: An explicitly named project that the fresh membership snapshot contains is the whole happy path: the record is stamped from the connection, not from anything the caller asserted about itself.
A saved CLI selection is a caller default the Server still verifies; it is never Server execution state, and it admits exactly like a request would.
When the caller names a project explicitly, the saved selection is not consulted at all — a stale selection can never redirect an explicit request.
A Solar submission's sealed input already names its project, so it needs no selection and a disagreeing selection is simply not used rather than refused.
Naming the same project the sealed bytes name is not a conflict; it is the ordinary explicit Solar submission and it admits.
A Solar submit whose sealed input was prepared for one project while the caller names another is refused scope_mismatch, and the refusal names only the project the caller already knows.

refusal.message: this request is for project-b, but its sealed input was prepared for another project

cases.why: No requested project, no saved selection and no sealed input means there is nothing to verify; the kernel refuses rather than inventing a default from process state.

refusal.message: name a project, or select one first

cases.why: A project outside the caller's verified membership is refused even though the caller named it explicitly: a caller-supplied id never grants access.

cases.why: A snapshot stamped after the host's clock is treated as unusable rather than eternally fresh, so a clock slip cannot extend a revoked membership.

cases.why: An account with no authorized projects admits nothing; an empty snapshot is a real answer, never an unconstrained one.

cases.why: The same key, project, operation and input bytes is an idempotent resubmit: the context already admitted comes back unchanged, so a retry never creates a second scope or re-stamps the admission time.
A key that already names one project cannot be reused to reach another; this is the retry rule that stops a reused key from borrowing another project's result.

refusal.message: that idempotency key already names another project or operation

cases.why: The durable job id is a digest of owner, lane and key, so the same key used for a different operation would collide with it; the scope of a key covers its operation as well as its project.

refusal.message: that idempotency key already names another project or operation

cases.why: Same key, same project, different bytes: the caller is trying to overwrite an existing result, which is refused rather than silently accepted or silently reused.

refusal.message: that idempotency key was admitted with different input bytes

cases.why: A stored record for this key that belongs to another account is a fence, not a reuse: the Server never lets one principal continue another's admitted work.

refusal.message: that key was admitted under another authenticated identity

cases.why: Canary and stable keep separate state; a key admitted on one lane is not the same key on the other even for the same account.

refusal.message: that key was admitted under another authenticated identity

cases.why: A credential bound to another gateway audience is another authority; the deployment is part of the principal fence and is checked before any reuse.

refusal.message: that key was admitted under another authenticated identity

cases.why: Probing a key while naming a project the caller cannot see must answer the project refusal, never the key refusal: otherwise reusing keys would disclose which projects hold work.

refusal.message: that project is not visible to this connection

cases.why: A record handed in for this key but stamped with another job id is corrupt host state, not a reusable admission; the kernel refuses rather than binding the caller to the wrong job.

cases.why: A stored context that no longer validates never becomes a fresh admission by accident; it is named corrupt so the host repairs it deliberately.

cases.why: The client label is caller-influenced text that ends up in a durable row, so it is bounded at admission and refused by name rather than truncated.

cases.why: The operation vocabulary is closed: a Server cannot be talked into admitting an operation the contract does not name.

refusal.message: execution context field operation is not a bounded value

cases.why: Every context binds the exact input bytes by sha256; anything that is not a 64-character lowercase digest cannot bind anything and is refused.

refusal.message: execution context field input_sha256 is not a bounded value

cases.why: A key with a control character would corrupt logs and durable rows; keys are trimmed, bounded and control-free before they can name a scope.

refusal.message: execution context field idempotency_key is not a bounded value

cases.why: There are exactly two lanes. A principal claiming a third has no verifiable deployment state and is refused before any project is resolved.

refusal.message: execution context field principal.lane is not a bounded value

cases.why: now_ms is an input so the decision is pure; a host that forgets it has a bug, and a bug is a hard error rather than something to relay to a client.

expected.error: admission needs the host's clock in now_ms

cases.why: Report generation for a second project is the overlapping work the contract demands, so it carries a context of its own exactly like Solar does.
A layer read is an operation too: its request id is its job id and its digest binds the exact request, so status and visibility work the same way for reads.
A layer write against an explicitly named project proves /v1/layers is admitted through the same owner as compute, not through a process-wide selection.
Transformer processing carries no project inside its request by design, which is exactly why an admitted context must supply one from a verified selection.
The account that admitted the work sees it without narrowing to a project: reconnection recovers a caller's jobs by stable id, not by whatever is selected now.
Narrowing a listing to the job's own project is the ordinary per-project query and stays visible.
install_id is recorded for provenance but is never a visibility fence, so the same account reconnecting from another machine still recovers its own durable work.
Another account asking about a known id gets the same three words an unknown id gets, so an id leaked out of a log discloses nothing about who owns it.

cases.why: A retry re-runs the same admitted work; it may not silently re-scope it to whatever project is selected at retry time. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.

After a Server restart the queue is reopened from durable rows, and reopening is not re-admission: the context is exactly the one stored. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
A worker claiming a job inherits the job's context; the worker's own environment contributes nothing to it. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.

Publication is where a wrong project would actually write into someone else's store, so the context it publishes under is the admitted one. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
Cancellation is an authorized action on a job, not a context change; the record it acts on is unchanged. The absurd now_ms proves the answer does not depend on the clock.
The identity function still refuses what is not a context: a row damaged on disk is named rather than carried forward into an effect.

refusal.message: execution context field project is not a bounded value

cases.why: An idle host admits work; capacity is a bound on saturation, not a gate every request must argue with.
A full running pool never refuses a submission: the job queues. Confusing 'no free worker' with 'no room' would drop admitted work.
One project saturating its own queue is refused with typed guidance instead of unbounded allocation, and the guidance grows with the work already waiting.

refusal.message: this project already has 3 of 3 operations waiting

cases.why: The point of a per-project bound: while A is saturated, B is admitted normally. A long Solar run must leave room for printing.
Global saturation refuses everyone, including a project with nothing queued, and names only counts and limits — never another project.

refusal.message: the server queue is full (8 of 8 waiting)

cases.why: A project may exceed its running share while nothing else is waiting: the machine is used, not idled to defend a share nobody wants.
The fairness rule itself: the moment another project has queued work, a project already at its share stops taking new slots.

refusal.message: this project holds 2 of 2 running slots while other projects are waiting

cases.why: The project that was waiting claims freely, so fairness actually moves work rather than merely blocking the other one.
Every worker busy refuses the claim globally, whichever project asks, with retry guidance derived from the queue rather than from a clock.

refusal.message: every worker is busy (4 of 4 running)

cases.why: Limits are the host's own configuration, so a zero limit is a host bug and a hard error, never a typed refusal relayed to a client.
The ordinary restart: a row admitted under this slice already carries its context and is reopened exactly as it was stored.
Whatever is selected at restart time is irrelevant to a row that already recorded its project; this is the rule that stops a restart from re-homing work.
A Solar row written by a released Server has no context, but its sealed input names its project authoritatively, so recovery is exact rather than a guess.
A transformer row carries no project by design, so the caller's saved selection is the only honest source; the record says so in its provenance.
With nothing to recover a project from, the kernel refuses instead of guessing. Extending admission must not strand a released Server's queue in the wrong project.

refusal.message: that row predates execution contexts and no project was selected to recover it into
